Take-home Exercise 1: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio Analysis

Executive Summary

Trinh Minh Tam

2026-05-20

Introduction

“Leveraging visual analytics can potentially help investigate trends in underlying loss drivers, while data enrichment can help refine segmentation and underwriting strategy.” — Swiss Re, sigma 4/2019

Objectives:

  • Explore distributions of numerical and categorical portfolio variables
  • Statistically validate key factors driving profitability (loss ratio) and volatility (claim frequency)

📖 Full technical report →

This presentation summarises the visual analytics investigation of a real Spanish motor vehicle insurance portfolio. All analyses use non-parametric tests (Kruskal-Wallis, Mann-Whitney, chi-square) because the key metrics — loss ratio and claim frequency — are heavily right-skewed and zero-inflated. For full methodology, code, and complete results, refer to the technical report.

Dataset at a Glance

Source Mendeley Data — Spanish non-life motor insurer
Records 354,140 policy-year observations
Period 2022 – 2024
Variables 47 raw + 5 derived actuarial KPIs
After filtering 352,165 records (0.6% removed — LR > 50 outliers)

Three core KPIs derived:

KPI Formula Measures
Loss Ratio Incurred ÷ Premium Profitability
Claim Frequency Claims ÷ Exposure Volatility
Avg. Severity Incurred ÷ Claims Cost per claim

The dataset covers three calendar years of a Spanish motor insurer’s full portfolio. Five actuarial KPIs were engineered using if_else() guards to avoid division-by-zero. 1,975 records with loss ratios above 50 were excluded — these represent catastrophic one-off events that would distort distribution plots. Full wrangling details at the technical report.

Portfolio Composition

CC is the dominant product, representing over half of all policies every year. COMP_E is the second-largest segment. Portfolio volumes are broadly stable across 2022–2024 with a modest increase in 2024, consistent with a mature, well-retained book growing at a measured pace. COMP_N is near-absent, indicating strong market preference for the excess variant (COMP_E) over the no-excess variant.

Portfolio Risk Profile

96.4% of policyholders carry a Good bonus score — a very low-risk base. New Business dominates at 69.3% versus Portfolio at 30.7%, which likely reflects how first-year policies are classified in this dataset. The portfolio is predominantly urban (53.8%) and inland (64.6%), consistent with the Spanish vehicle fleet distribution.

Loss Ratio: All Medians Are Zero

Because most policies generate no claim in any given year, all five policy types share a median loss ratio of 0.00. The meaningful risk differences lie in the upper tail — COMP_N has the widest, flattest distribution with the most mass stretching beyond the break-even line of 1.0, confirming it as the highest profitability-risk product. TP policies are almost entirely spiked at zero. This zero-inflation context is critical for interpreting all subsequent statistical tests — the tests detect tail differences, not median differences.

📖 Full ridgeline analysis →

Profitability Driver 1: Bonus Score

Despite all medians being 0.00, all three pairwise comparisons are statistically significant after BH correction — including Good vs Neutral (p ≈ 0.00002). The Kruskal-Wallis test detects differences in rank distributions, not medians. The Bad segment has a visibly heavier scatter of high loss ratio observations, meaning Bad-score policyholders disproportionately generate the portfolio’s large, unprofitable claims. Bonus score is the single strongest available profitability predictor.

📖 Full bonus score analysis →

Profitability Driver 2: Policy Type

Again all medians are 0.00, but the rank distributions differ significantly across product lines. COMP_N (comprehensive, no excess) has the heaviest tail — its broad coverage scope and absence of a deductible removes the financial barrier to small claims. COMP_E is significantly less risky than COMP_N, showing the deductible acts as a partial brake. TP and TPG are the most profitable lines with the narrowest distributions. These findings support differential pricing between COMP_E and COMP_N.

📖 Full policy type analysis →

Profitability Driver 3: Driver Age

The Spearman correlation is negative and statistically significant — older drivers tend to generate lower loss ratios. The effect is most visible for drivers under 30, where the scatter shows a clear concentration of elevated loss ratio observations. The marginal histograms reveal the right-skewed, zero-inflated nature of loss ratio and the bell-shaped age distribution simultaneously. Spearman is appropriate because neither variable is normally distributed.

📖 Full driver age analysis →

Volatility: Claim Frequency by Policy Type

All medians are 0.00 (zero-inflated). However, the rank-based test confirms that comprehensive policies have a significantly heavier upper tail (χ²=570.91, p≈0). COMP_N shows a significantly higher frequency distribution than COMP_E (p≈0) — the absence of excess removes the financial hurdle for minor claims. Combined with severity, this confirms comprehensive products are driven by both higher frequency and higher severity: a compounding effect. For bonus score frequency analysis, only the Bad–Good comparison is significant (weaker effect).

📖 Full volatility analysis →

Claim Incidence: Bonus Score vs Fuel Type

These ggbarstats charts show binary claim incidence proportions — unlike the ggbetweenstats charts, these are not affected by zero-inflation in the same way. Bad-score policyholders have a 22% claim rate versus 14% for Good (1.6× difference), highly significant. Diesel vehicles have a 15% claim incidence versus 12% for gasoline — this is largely confounded by diesel carrying more comprehensive cover (more claimable event types), so fuel type is a proxy for vehicle profile rather than a direct risk driver.

📖 Full association analysis →

Vehicle Brand Risk Landscape

The treemap communicates two dimensions simultaneously — portfolio concentration (tile size) and profitability heterogeneity (colour). The dominant brands by volume are Spanish and European mass-market brands (RENAULT, CITROEN, PEUGEOT, VOLKSWAGEN, FORD). Smaller tiles in orange-red shading represent brands with fewer policies but elevated loss ratios, consistent with higher per-claim repair costs on luxury or performance vehicles. This view directly informs underwriting appetite by brand.

Key Findings

Profitability (Loss Ratio)

  • 🔴 Bad bonus score → heaviest loss ratio tail across all groups
  • 🔴 COMP_N / COMP_E → widest upper-tail distributions (all medians = 0.00)
  • 🟡 Young drivers (<25) → broadest, most right-tailed distributions
  • 🟡 Urban circulation → statistically higher loss ratio than rural
  • 🟢 TP / TPG → tightest, lowest-risk distributions

Volatility (Claim Frequency)

  • 🔴 COMP_N > COMP_E > CC > TP — frequency tail ordering mirrors loss ratio
  • 🔴 Diesel claim incidence (15%) > Gasoline (12%) — driven by coverage mix
  • 🟡 Bad bonus claim incidence (22%) vs Good (14%) — 1.6× difference
  • 🟡 Only Bad–Good frequency comparison significant (weaker bonus effect)
  • 🟢 Good bonus (96.4% of portfolio) provides strong natural protection

Implication: Bonus score and policy type are the dominant pricing factors. COMP_N warrants a pricing adequacy review — its no-excess structure drives both higher frequency and higher severity. Driver age and circulation area provide incremental lift as secondary factors.

The investigation confirms that insurance loss data is inherently zero-inflated — most policies have no claims — so median-based summaries are uninformative. All meaningful risk differentiation occurs in the upper tail of the distribution, which is why non-parametric rank tests and distributional visualisations are essential. Bonus score is the single strongest predictor across both profitability and volatility dimensions.
